one_liner: University of Rochester preprint: a CBET laser-plasma simulation written in Rust ran up to 5.6x faster than the group's C++ version.
what_it_does: arXiv 2410.19146 (October 2024, physics.comp-ph; search snippets say it was submitted to an Elsevier journal, publication not confirmed) compares C++ and Rust implementations of a Cross Beam Energy Transfer (CBET) simulation, the energy exchange where high-intensity laser beams cross in a plasma. It also reports a parallel Rust version and runs test cases with different mesh sizes; one figure caption seen in a snippet is 'CBET sequential version runtime for 2500 x 2500 mesh'. It is a case study, not a library: no source code for either version was found on github.com, and the paper itself could not be opened here.
how_it_is_fast: Not documented in anything readable here: the paper (arxiv.org abs, html, pdf), its ResearchGate copy and every mirror tried are unreachable, so the authors' explanation was not read. The only concrete design difference reported, through search snippets of the Lobsters discussion, is data layout: the C++ version uses struct-of-arrays and the Rust version array-of-structs, and the authors argue this alone does not explain the gap. The same discussion says both versions were fresh implementations and that the C++ code was modified to resemble the Rust code, so any speedup mixes language, compiler (rustc versus an unnamed C++ compiler) and implementation choices.
when_to_use: As an anecdote when weighing a C++ to Rust port of a mesh-based scientific code: a small group reported the Rust version was not slower, and was at least 1.6x faster on smaller cases per snippets.
As a pointer that safe parallel Rust (the paper's parallel version) can speed a sequential physics kernel up further with little effort, if you plan to parallelise during the port anyway.
Not as a library: there is nothing to link or vendor, so it only informs a language decision.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Rust is generally faster than C++: same-algorithm studies point the other way (ASE 2022 'Towards Understanding the Runtime Performance of Rust' found Rust about 1.77x slower than C on average; arXiv 2209.09127 'Is Rust C++-fast?' found near parity with a small Rust deficit).
To predict the gain for your own code: compilers, flags, CPU model, per-case runtimes and the reason for the gap were not seen, and no code exists to rerun it.
As peer-reviewed evidence: it is an arXiv preprint; no journal or conference version was found.

As a comparison of tuned C++: the C++ version was the group's own and was changed to resemble the Rust code (Lobsters snippet), so a tuned C++ implementation with its own data layout was never the baseline.

integration.form: source-drop (not available: paper only, no public code found)
integration.min_toolchain: not documented (rustc and C++ compiler versions not seen)
integration.platforms: not documented beyond an AMD EPYC test machine (model not seen) and at least one other machine
integration.thread_safety: not documented (the parallel Rust version's threading approach was not seen)

gotchas: Harness flaw: the two versions do not share a data layout (C++ struct-of-arrays, Rust array-of-structs, per a Lobsters comment summarised in a search snippet), so the measured gap is partly an implementation effect rather than a language effect; the authors reportedly argue layout alone does not explain it.

Unresolved: the abstract (search snippet) says some test cases showed up to a 5.6x increase and that parallel Rust 'can further improve' performance, but a Hacker News commenter (snippet) read the paper as about 1.6x from the near-identical sequential port with the larger gain coming from the parallel Rust version. If 5.6x compares parallel Rust with sequential C++, it is not a language comparison at all.

A Lobsters commenter (snippet) found the paper unclear about who wrote which implementation and saw no code link; two earlier searches and this pass (github.com topics 'cbet' and 'laser-plasma', author user pages) found no repository.
A 1.6x to 5.6x gap between equally optimised sequential C++ and Rust is unusual; without flags (for example -O2 versus -O3, -ffast-math, aliasing assumptions) it cannot be attributed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Cite it only as a scientific-computing anecdote; for reproducible Rust-versus-C++ evidence prefer ckmeans (vendored Ckmeans.1d.dp C++ baseline, Criterion runs) or ixy-languages (same driver design in C and Rust, cycle counts), whose code and baselines can be checked.
verified_claims_summary: Per search snippets only, the Rust CBET simulation ran at least 1.6x as fast as the authors' C++ version on smaller meshes and up to 5.6x faster on a large mesh (2500 x 2500 is the mesh named in one figure caption) on an AMD EPYC machine of unknown model, with compilers and flags unknown; a parallel Rust version was faster still, and whether the 5.6x figure is sequential is disputed in discussion.
status_note: Reference-only arXiv preprint (2024) with no public code; the paper, its ResearchGate copy, the Lobsters and Hacker News threads and the authors' pages were all unreachable here, so this entry rests on search snippets and stays a candidate for a paper-access retier.
